newsitem.title: USA: Those who need key heart test don't get it - study.
newsitem.headline: Those who need key heart test don't get it - study.

text.p: Patients who stand to benefit most from an exploratory technique known as heart angiography often do not get the test from their doctors, according to a study in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.
Instead, patients with healthier hearts are more likely to get the test, especially if they are being treated in a large hospital or a for-profit hospital, the study concluded.

Angiography involves snaking a tube into the heart, injecting dye through the tube and using X-rays to track the flow of the dye. The test, among other things, reveals the location and extent of blocked heart arteries.

A team led by Dr. Louise Pilote of Montreal General Hospital found that older heart patients and patients who are more likely to develop complications during the test are less likely to have the procedure prescribed for them. As a result the people most likely to be helped by angiography often are not given the test.

Their findings are based on an analysis of 21,772 heart attack patients who volunteered for a study originally designed to see which of two drug treatments worked best for opening a clogged heart artery.

The Pilote team found that while 76 percent of patients under 73 received angiography, only 53 percent of those 73 years old and over got the test. The older the patient, the lower the likelihood that they would get the test.
Younger heart attack patients with simple heart problems are less likely to need angiography. "Patients with complications have the most to gain from this procedure," they said.

The team also found that rural and teaching hospitals were less likely to do an angiography than larger hospitals and for-profit hospitals. And if the hospital had the equipment available, the test was more likely to be recommended.

The researchers said doctors apparently either misunderstand the benefits of angiography for older patients or are giving the test to younger people "because they simply identify with younger patients."
